contents.html: This report summarizes the feedback received by the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things (IoT) program at the in-person and hybrid workshop on "Updating Manufacturer Guidance for Securable Connected Product Development" held in December 2024. The purpose of this workshop was to consider how to update Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers (NIST Internal Report (IR) 8259) based on concepts in risk management, operational technology concerns, product end of life concerns and recent trends in IoT cybersecurity and privacy. Over time, the NIST volume of work has built upon the concepts introduced in NIST IR 8259,to add technical (NIST IR 8259A) and nontechnical (NIST IR 8259B) concepts to help manufacturers and customers consider the cybersecurity of IoT devices. The NIST IR 8259 series has been used to inform and develop subsequent publications that elaborate on IoT cybersecurity across sectors and use cases (e.g., federal agency uses cases reflected in NIST SP 800-213 and consumer use cases reflected in NIST IR 8425 and the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark).
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、2024年12月に対面形式およびハイブリッド形式で開催された「セキュリティ保護可能な接続製品の開発に向けた製造者向けガイダンス更新」ワークショップで、NISTのInternet of Things（IoT）サイバーセキュリティプログラムが受けたフィードバックを要約しています。このワークショップの目的は、リスク管理、運用技術に関する懸念、製品のサポート終了に関する懸念、IoTのサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーの最近の動向に関する概念に基づき、Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers（NIST Internal Report（IR）8259）をどのように更新するかを検討することでした。NISTの一連の取り組みは、時間をかけてNIST IR 8259で導入された概念を土台とし、製造者と顧客がIoTデバイスのサイバーセキュリティを検討するのに役立つ技術的な概念（NIST IR 8259A）および非技術的な概念（NIST IR 8259B）を加えてきました。NIST IR 8259シリーズは、分野やユースケースをまたぐIoTサイバーセキュリティを詳しく説明する後続の刊行物（たとえば、NIST SP 800-213に反映された連邦政府機関のユースケースや、NIST IR 8425およびU.S. Cyber Trust Markに反映された消費者向けユースケース）の策定に活用されてきました。

contents.html: On December 4th, 2024, NIST hosted a workshop titled “Workshop on Updating Manufacturer Guidance for Securable Connected Product Development” to introduce and discuss potential areas to update as the NIST Cybersecurity for Internet of Things (IoT) program revises Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers, NIST IR 8259. The workshop was structured into two portions: a morning colloquium of plenary speakers and afternoon discussion sessions to dive deeper into the topics highlighted in the morning. The workshop yielded many discussions and significant feedback for NIST. This report summarizes what was discussed at the workshop and provides these insights to the broader public.
contents.html_ja: 2024年12月4日（December 4th）に、NIST は、NIST の Cybersecurity for Internet of Things（IoT）プログラムが Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers, NIST IR 8259 を改訂するにあたって更新の対象となり得る分野を紹介し議論するため、「セキュリティ保護可能な接続製品の開発に向けた製造者向けガイダンス更新ワークショップ（Workshop on Updating Manufacturer Guidance for Securable Connected Product Development）」と題するワークショップを主催しました。ワークショップは二部構成で、午前は全体講演者による講演会、午後は午前に取り上げたトピックを掘り下げる討論セッションでした。ワークショップでは多くの議論があり、NIST に対して重要なフィードバックが寄せられました。本報告書は、ワークショップで議論された内容を要約し、これらの知見を広く一般に提供するものです。

1. Government actions to support strengthening IoT cybersecurity need to be coordinated with industry.
2. The use of robust frameworks and the adoption of open standards are crucial for effectively managing risks across heterogeneous environments.
3. The dynamic nature of threats requires more context aware inputs, more proactive tracking and mitigation measures, and more examination into the inputs of the threat modeling approach.
4. There are market opportunities to securely design the next wave of products with cybersecurity through end of life and instill incentives into the maintenance of existing products.
5. The balance of shared responsibility between manufacturers and users for improving security varies by sector and needs the right incentives for both.
6. There are broad challenges to integrating privacy objectives into IoT cybersecurity risk management.
7. There is an increased awareness for evolving cybersecurity responsibilities across the players of the IoT ecosystem from manufacturers to users of the ecosystem.

contents.html: David Keppler and Jack Cyprus, both from the MITRE Corporation, discussed building more secure devices through threat modeling with MITRE EMB3D<sup>1</sup>. They emphasized that threat modeling is crucial for identifying potential vulnerabilities and determining appropriate security measures. This process, which is increasingly used in industries such as industrial automation, automotive, and medical, involves defining the device, identifying key components and trust boundaries, and measuring the return on investment (ROI) of defenses.
contents.html_ja: MITRE Corporation の David Keppler と Jack Cyprus は、MITRE EMB3D<sup>1</sup> を用いた脅威モデリングによる、より安全なデバイスの構築について論じました。両氏は、脅威モデリングが、潜在的な脆弱性を特定し、適切なセキュリティ対策を決定するうえで重要であると強調しました。このプロセスは、産業オートメーション、自動車、医療などの業界で利用が増えており、デバイスの定義、主要なコンポーネントと信頼境界の特定、防御策の投資対効果（ROI）の測定を含みます。

contents.html: There are various tools and processes for threat modeling, such as adversary models and attack trees. One prominent model, the MITRE EMB3D, fills gaps in existing data sources and offers a consistent understanding of threats and mitigations. This model categorizes threats based on device properties, such as hardware, system software, application software, and networking. It also includes references to the CWE and CVE databases for additional information and threat details.
contents.html_ja: 脅威モデリングには、敵対者モデルや攻撃ツリーなど、さまざまなツールとプロセスがあります。代表的なモデルの一つである MITRE EMB3D は、既存のデータソースの空白を埋め、脅威と緩和策について一貫した理解を提供します。このモデルは、ハードウェア、システムソフトウェア、アプリケーションソフトウェア、ネットワークなどのデバイスの特性に基づいて脅威を分類します。また、追加情報や脅威の詳細のために、CWE と CVE のデータベースへの参照も含みます。

contents.html: The EMB3D model provides a common language for device vendors, users, and security researchers to communicate threats and mitigations. It includes three mitigation tiers— foundational, intermediate, and leading—that guide actions throughout a device's lifecycle. These mitigations are grounded in real-world information and provide a defensive starting point as well as steps for ongoing security improvements. By adopting a comprehensive threat modeling process like EMB3D, organizations can better protect their devices against potential threats and build more secure systems.
contents.html_ja: EMB3D モデルは、デバイスのベンダー、利用者、セキュリティ研究者が脅威と緩和策を伝え合うための共通言語を提供します。デバイスのライフサイクル全体にわたる行動を導く、基礎、中級、先進の 3 つの緩和策の段階を含みます。これらの緩和策は実世界の情報に基づいており、防御の出発点と、継続的なセキュリティ改善のための手順を提供します。EMB3D のような包括的な脅威モデリングプロセスを採用することで、組織は、潜在的な脅威からデバイスをよりよく保護し、より安全なシステムを構築できます。

contents.html: Matthew Rogers from CISA presented on the agency’s Secure-By-Design pledge <sup>2</sup>and related efforts. Secure-by-design incentivizes security professionals to drive meaningful security changes and equips consumers with the knowledge to demand necessary security features. Establishing a secure and upgradeable foundation is crucial to avoid legacy infrastructure issues. Shared responsibility between asset owners and device manufacturers is essential, as software vulnerabilities are increasing and basic, preventable vulnerabilities can cause significant harm.

contents.html: Security is a collective responsibility involving manufacturers, integrators, and asset owners and operators. CISA helps clarify security roles and ensures all parties uphold their responsibilities. The key component of secure by design is seeing where manufacturers can embed cyber security from the start to make it more difficult or impossible for an integrator or asset owner to open a cyber security risk.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティは、製造者、インテグレータ、資産の所有者と運用者が関わる共同の責任です。CISA は、セキュリティ上の役割を明確にし、すべての当事者が責任を果たすようにする助けとなります。セキュア・バイ・デザインの重要な要素は、製造者が最初からサイバーセキュリティを組み込める箇所を見極め、インテグレータや資産所有者がサイバーセキュリティリスクを生じさせることを困難に、または不可能にすることです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p10と一致

contents.html: Current US critical infrastructure contains legacy systems without security functionality that inherently complicate adding security today. Infrastructure improvement options include the present ‘Bubble Boy’ method, which segments all traffic, targeted improvements, and the 'rip and replace' method. Secure operational technology (OT) devices need to be available to provide that defense in depth, so that any failures in segmentation do not result in total compromise. Secure-by-design for OT considers threat categories like vulnerability handling and data protection. It emphasizes open standards and autonomy at the asset and operator level. Resilience features should resemble those in the enterprise space, including secure communications, resilience, logging, and end-device capabilities.
contents.html_ja: 現在の米国の重要インフラには、セキュリティ機能のないレガシーシステムが含まれており、現在セキュリティを追加することが本質的に難しくなっています。インフラ改善の選択肢には、すべての通信を分離する現行の「Bubble Boy」方式、的を絞った改善、'rip and replace'（全面置き換え）方式があります。多層防御を提供するために、安全な運用技術（OT）デバイスが利用可能である必要があり、セグメンテーションに不備があっても全面的な危殆化に至らないようにする必要があります。OT のセキュア・バイ・デザインでは、脆弱性への対応やデータ保護などの脅威カテゴリが考慮されます。資産および運用者のレベルで、オープンな標準と自律性が重視されます。レジリエンス機能は、安全な通信、レジリエンス、ログ記録、エンドデバイスの機能など、エンタープライズ領域のものに類似しているべきです。

contents.html: 2.3. Stacey Higginbotham, Fellow with Consumer Reports, presented, ‘Life in Maintenance Mode: What it means to keep connected devices secure.’
contents.html_ja: 2.3. Stacey Higginbotham（Consumer Reports フェロー）による講演『Life in Maintenance Mode: What it means to keep connected devices secure.』
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p10の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: Stacey Higginbotham of Consumer Reports noted that connected devices establish an ongoing relationship between the buyer, seller, and manufacturer. The lifetime of a connected product is often separate from its physical state. While physical products fail in visible ways, software degrades more quickly, often without consumer awareness. The industry also lacks adequate support for maintenance. Stacey’s discussion highlighted three key areas: zombie hordes of end of life devices, supported devices with unsupportive owners, and herd immunity against malicious actors.
contents.html_ja: Consumer Reports の Stacey Higginbotham は、接続デバイスが、購入者、販売者、製造者の間に継続的な関係を確立すると指摘しました。接続製品の寿命は、その物理的な状態とは別であることが多くあります。物理的な製品は目に見える形で故障しますが、ソフトウェアはより速く劣化し、消費者が気づかないことも多くあります。業界には、保守に対する十分なサポートもありません。Stacey の議論は、寿命末期のデバイスのゾンビの群れ、サポートされているのにサポートに非協力的な所有者、悪意のある行為者に対する集団免疫という 3 つの主要分野を取り上げました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p10と一致

contents.html: “Zombie devices” are those that no longer receive software support and security updates. Higginbotham noted that unsupportive owners can neglect cybersecurity issues, leading to vulnerabilities. Herd immunity in cybersecurity requires collective action from manufacturers and consumers. Most consumers are unaware or indifferent to the end of life status of their products, resulting in “zombie hordes”. Communicating end of life status and dates is crucial, including proactive notification to consumers, retailers, and third parties. Companies should track devices to address critical vulnerabilities and create structured options for off-ramping zombie devices.
contents.html_ja: 「ゾンビデバイス」とは、ソフトウェアのサポートとセキュリティ更新を受けられなくなったデバイスです。Higginbotham は、協力的でない所有者がサイバーセキュリティ上の問題を放置し、脆弱性につながり得ると指摘しました。サイバーセキュリティにおける集団免疫には、製造者と消費者の集団的な行動が必要です。ほとんどの消費者は、自分の製品の寿命末期の状態に気づいていないか、無関心であり、その結果「ゾンビの群れ」が生じます。寿命末期の状態と日付を伝えることは、消費者、小売業者、第三者への事前の通知を含め、極めて重要です。企業は、重大な脆弱性に対処するためにデバイスを追跡し、ゾンビデバイスの段階的廃止に向けた体系的な選択肢を作るべきです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p10と一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: unsupportive owners を「サポートを受けられない製品の所有者」と誤訳していた

contents.html: Higginbotham emphasized that company priorities often overlook device security. Manufacturers should implement vulnerability disclosure programs, track issues, conduct comprehensive security audits, and allocate budgets for security maintenance. Buyers must keep products updated or segmented, and legislation should clarify responsibility to ensure herd immunity. Companies should have a dedicated point of contact for security researchers and consider recalls for insecure devices. Stacey also addressed secure repairs, both before and after end of life. Good hardware should not end up in landfills, but unpatched zombie devices pose risks. Consumer Reports advocates for designing products for longevity, including features like hardware upgrades, crypto agility, and increased memory.
contents.html_ja: Higginbotham は、企業の優先事項がデバイスのセキュリティを見過ごしがちであると強調しました。製造者は、脆弱性開示プログラムを実施し、問題を追跡し、包括的なセキュリティ監査を行い、セキュリティ保守のための予算を割り当てるべきです。購入者は、製品を最新に保つか分離しておかなければならず、集団免疫を確保するために、法律で責任を明確にすべきです。企業は、セキュリティ研究者向けの専用の連絡窓口を持ち、安全でないデバイスのリコールを検討すべきです。Stacey は、寿命末期の前後を問わず、安全な修理についても取り上げました。良質なハードウェアが埋立地に行き着くべきではありませんが、パッチのないゾンビデバイスはリスクをもたらします。Consumer Reports は、ハードウェアのアップグレード、暗号アジリティ、メモリの増強といった機能を含め、長寿命を想定して製品を設計することを提唱しています。

contents.html: 2.4. Dylan Gilbert, NIST Privacy Engineering Program Lead, presented, ‘Getting Smart: An Overview of IoT Privacy’.
contents.html_ja: 2.4. Dylan Gilbert（NIST Privacy Engineering Program Lead）による講演『Getting Smart: An Overview of IoT Privacy』
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p11の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: Privacy is a complex and evolving concept that safeguards important values like human autonomy and dignity. It reflects various factors and individual preferences and is highly context-specific, differing between public and private activities. Effective privacy risk management must consider these contexts and the various ways to achieve privacy, such as seclusion, limiting observation, and controlling facets of identity.
contents.html_ja: プライバシーは、人間の自律や尊厳といった重要な価値を守る、複雑で進化する概念です。さまざまな要因や個人の好みを反映し、非常に文脈に依存して、公的な活動と私的な活動で異なります。効果的なプライバシーリスクマネジメントは、これらの文脈と、隔離、観察の制限、アイデンティティの側面の管理など、プライバシーを実現するさまざまな方法を考慮しなければなりません。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p11と一致

contents.html: Gilbert emphasized that privacy could drive innovation and serve as a market differentiator. However, organizations need to have honest and risk-informed discussions about how best to balance optimizing data utility while protecting individuals’ privacy, particularly in cases where privacy risk interacts with other risk domains such as cybersecurity. The NIST Privacy Framework helps organizations understand the relationship between privacy and cybersecurity risks in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT). Problematic data actions, such as deriving inferences about individuals, can pose significant privacy risks, particularly in consumer IoT.
contents.html_ja: Gilbert は、プライバシーがイノベーションを促し、市場での差別化要因になり得ると強調しました。ただし、組織は、データの有用性を最適化しつつ個人のプライバシーを保護するバランスを最もよくとる方法について、特に、プライバシーリスクがサイバーセキュリティなどの他のリスク領域と相互作用する場合には、率直でリスクに基づいた議論を行う必要があります。NIST Privacy Framework は、組織がモノのインターネット（IoT）の文脈で、プライバシーとサイバーセキュリティのリスクの関係を理解する助けとなります。個人に関する推論を導き出すなど、問題のあるデータ処理は、特に消費者向け IoT で、重大なプライバシーリスクをもたらし得ます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p11と一致

contents.html: A key factor in managing privacy risks is an organization’s role in the data processing ecosystem, which includes the complex relationships among entities involved in data processing. An organization's role(s) in the IoT ecosystem can affect its legal obligations and the measures it should take to manage privacy risk. High-level goals for mitigating cybersecurity and privacy risks include protecting device security, data security, and individual privacy. The privacy engineering objectives of predictability, manageability, and disassociability can be useful to meet these goals by supporting the determination of privacy capabilities in IoT products.
contents.html_ja: プライバシーリスクを管理する際の重要な要因は、データ処理のエコシステムにおける組織の役割で、これにはデータ処理に関わる事業体間の複雑な関係が含まれます。IoT エコシステムにおける組織の役割は、その法的義務と、プライバシーリスクを管理するためにとるべき措置に影響し得ます。サイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクを緩和する高レベルの目標には、デバイスのセキュリティ、データのセキュリティ、個人のプライバシーの保護が含まれます。予測可能性、管理可能性、非関連付け性（disassociability）というプライバシーエンジニアリングの目標は、IoT 製品におけるプライバシー機能の決定を支えることで、これらの目標を満たすのに役立ちます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p11と一致

contents.html: Gilbert also discussed specific privacy risks related to IoT, such as interactions with the physical world leading to reputational harm or safety issues. Data processing might exceed the product's intended scope, and access, management, and monitoring features could result in loss of trust and economic loss. Additionally, privacy capability availability, efficiency, and effectiveness are crucial to prevent issues like discrimination and to maintain trust. IoT products need the capabilities to support configurations such as remote activation, prevention, and data minimization.
contents.html_ja: Gilbert は、物理世界とのやり取りが評判の毀損や安全上の問題につながることなど、IoT に関する具体的なプライバシーリスクについても論じました。データ処理が製品の意図した範囲を超える可能性があり、アクセス、管理、監視の機能が、信頼の喪失や経済的損失をもたらし得ます。さらに、プライバシー機能の可用性、効率、有効性は、差別などの問題を防ぎ、信頼を維持するために極めて重要です。IoT 製品には、リモートでの有効化、予防、データ最小化といった構成を支える機能が必要です。

contents.html: The following takeaways are the ideas, observations, and suggestions that NIST heard from workshop participants and that received significant support from attendees and/or panelists. This workshop was not a forum for developing consensus; rather, the takeaways represent recurrent themes which emerged during the event—not formal positions taken by attendees or participants. This document cannot capture every thought, opinion, and suggestion provided during the sessions. This is an attempt to capture major themes. The takeaways do not represent specific NIST recommendations or guidelines; rather, they provide important feedback to the program and serve as a basis for future conversations with the community.
contents.html_ja: 以下の要点は、NIST がワークショップ参加者から聞いた考え、所見、提案であり、出席者やパネリストから大きな支持を得たものです。このワークショップは合意形成の場ではありませんでした。要点は、イベント中に繰り返し現れたテーマを表すものであり、出席者や参加者がとった正式な立場ではありません。本文書は、セッション中に示されたすべての考え、意見、提案を網羅できるものではありません。これは主要なテーマを捉える試みです。要点は NIST の具体的な勧告やガイドラインを表すものではなく、プログラムへの重要なフィードバックを提供し、コミュニティとの今後の対話の基礎となるものです。

contents.html: Government actions to support strengthening IoT cybersecurity need to be coordinated with industry.
contents.html_ja: IoT サイバーセキュリティの強化を支える政府の取り組みは、産業界と連携させる必要があります。

contents.html: The government plays a crucial role in strengthening IoT cybersecurity in coordination with industry, in areas such as promoting balancing security with operational needs, and consumer awareness through effective communication and education. In these efforts, the government must work collaboratively with industry stakeholders, recognizing its own limitations while providing expert support for broader cybersecurity objectives.
contents.html_ja: 政府は、セキュリティと運用上のニーズのバランスをとることの促進や、効果的なコミュニケーションと教育による消費者の意識向上といった分野で、産業界と連携して IoT サイバーセキュリティを強化するうえで、重要な役割を果たします。こうした取り組みでは、政府は産業界の利害関係者と協力して取り組まなければならず、自らの限界を認識しつつ、より広いサイバーセキュリティの目標に対して専門的な支援を提供します。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p12と一致

contents.html: The speakers highlighted the government's initiatives like Secure by Design and programs like the US Cyber Trust Mark as crucial to encourage industry to balance security requirements with operational constraints in a range of environments from Operational Control (OT) to consumer products. Under such initiatives and programs, government and industry efforts need to align to ensure the effective implementation of cybersecurity measures. Participants voiced support for a unified whole-of-government approach to address the challenges posed across different sectors and use cases ensuring that security initiatives are both comprehensive and adaptable. Discussions highlighted that, while the government can support broad objectives and promote improved cybersecurity, it should be flexible concerning specific product security measures, which are the responsibility of manufacturers.
contents.html_ja: 講演者は、運用技術（OT）から消費者向け製品までのさまざまな環境で、産業界がセキュリティ要件と運用上の制約のバランスをとることを促すために、Secure by Designなどの政府の取り組みや、US Cyber Trust Markなどのプログラムが極めて重要であると強調しました。こうした取り組みやプログラムの下では、サイバーセキュリティ対策を効果的に実施するために、政府と産業界の取り組みを整合させる必要があります。参加者は、異なる分野やユースケースにわたる課題に対処し、セキュリティの取り組みが包括的であると同時に適応可能であることを確保するために、政府全体で統一したアプローチをとることへの支持を表明しました。議論では、政府は広範な目標を支援し、サイバーセキュリティの改善を促進できる一方で、製造者の責任である個別の製品セキュリティ対策については柔軟であるべきです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p12と一致

contents.html: Instead, participants recommended that the government could provide top-level support for broader cybersecurity objectives, integrating planning approaches to navigate the complexities of different sectors. Tools like effective consumer education awareness campaigns may drive better security practices to ensure consumers are well-informed about cybersecurity measures as they evolve. Participants agreed that one key aspect of government involvement is effective communication, which the participants agreed should be action-based messages directed at consumers. For example, simplifying communication and facilitating customer outreach are ways to promote awareness and understanding of cybersecurity practices. Government-led programs for consumer education were seen as vital by the audience in driving consumer engagement and encouraging consumers to value secure products. It was noted that “one size fits all communications” does not address the varying levels of knowledge in the general public.
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、むしろ政府が、より広いサイバーセキュリティの目標に対して最上位レベルの支援を提供し、異なる分野の複雑さに対応する計画のアプローチを統合できるのではないかと提案しました。効果的な消費者教育の啓発キャンペーンなどのツールは、消費者が進化するサイバーセキュリティ対策について十分な情報を得られるようにすることで、より優れたセキュリティの実践を促す可能性があります。参加者は、政府の関与の重要な側面の一つが効果的なコミュニケーションであることに同意し、それは消費者に向けた行動を促すメッセージであるべきだとしました。たとえば、コミュニケーションを簡素化し、顧客へのアウトリーチを促進することは、サイバーセキュリティの実践に対する認識と理解を高める方法です。政府主導の消費者教育プログラムは、消費者の関与を促し、消費者が安全な製品を重視するよう促すうえで不可欠であると、聴衆に見なされました。「万人向けの画一的なコミュニケーション」は、一般の人々の知識水準の違いに対応できないことも指摘されました。

contents.html: Broad understanding of cybersecurity information and what to do with it is essential for improvement in U.S. cybersecurity. This means tailoring the message to the expected audience and collaborating with industry to move toward a more robust cybersecurity ecosystem.

contents.html: Throughout the workshop, the importance of established frameworks and open standards was discussed as beneficial to enhancing IoT security and reducing threats. Real-world examples showcased how these tools can effectively mitigate cybersecurity threats while considering interactions between mitigations and device properties. It was noted that there are emerging examples of standards organizations using threat frameworks to discuss risk management.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップを通じて、確立されたフレームワークとオープンな標準の重要性が、IoT セキュリティの強化と脅威の低減に有益であるとして論じられました。実世界の例により、緩和策とデバイスの特性との相互作用を考慮しながら、これらのツールがサイバーセキュリティの脅威を効果的に軽減できることが示されました。標準化団体が、リスクマネジメントを論じるために脅威フレームワークを使う例が出てきていることも指摘されました。

contents.html: Open standards were discussed as crucial in fostering interoperability and resilience, particularly within OT and ICS environments. Participants underscored the value of standards in making vulnerability advisories more actionable through enhanced communication across various systems. The need for clear, informative references and robust use case examples was also highlighted, emphasizing their role in clarifying specific points and supporting industry best practices.
contents.html_ja: オープンな標準は、特に OT および ICS 環境で、相互運用性とレジリエンスを促進するうえで極めて重要であると論じられました。参加者は、さまざまなシステム間のコミュニケーションを強化することで、脆弱性アドバイザリをより実用的にするという標準の価値を強調しました。明確で有益な参照と堅牢なユースケースの例の必要性も強調され、特定の点を明確にし、業界のベストプラクティスを支えるうえでのそれらの役割が重視されました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13と一致

contents.html: As topics of discussion, privacy compliance and risk management emerged as important yet distinct areas of focus. The discussions noted the challenges in defining authority for privacy and managing privacy risks and the value of frameworks such as the NIST Privacy Framework to address these challenges. Additionally, there was a recognized need for a product baseline and specific security controls at varying levels to enhance overall cybersecurity efforts. Participants noted that clear and direct communication, along with formalized sections within documents, would further support the effective implementation of best practices and ensure a comprehensive approach to cybersecurity.
contents.html_ja: 議論のトピックとして、プライバシーコンプライアンスとリスクマネジメントは、重要でありながら別個の焦点領域として浮かび上がりました。議論では、プライバシーに関する権限を定義し、プライバシーリスクを管理することの課題と、これらの課題に対処するうえでの NIST Privacy Framework などのフレームワークの価値が指摘されました。さらに、サイバーセキュリティの取り組み全体を強化するために、製品のベースラインと、さまざまなレベルでの具体的なセキュリティ管理策が必要であることが認識されました。参加者は、明確で直接的なコミュニケーションと、文書内の正式化された節が、ベストプラクティスの効果的な実施をさらに支え、サイバーセキュリティへの包括的なアプローチを確保すると指摘しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13と一致

contents.html: 3.3. Addressing Emerging Threats and Vulnerabilities
contents.html_ja: 3.3. 新たな脅威と脆弱性への対処
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: The dynamic nature of threats requires more context aware inputs, more proactive tracking and mitigation measures, and more examination into the inputs of the threat modeling approach.
contents.html_ja: 脅威の動的な性質により、状況を踏まえた入力情報の増加、より能動的な追跡と緩和策、脅威モデリング手法の入力情報の一層の検証が必要です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13の網掛けの太字の要点文（表1の行と同文）。表ではなく段落に直す

contents.html: During the workshop, discussions highlighted the dynamic nature of threats, emphasizing that threats should be examined within their specific contexts rather than by sector. Participants noted that this approach ensures a comprehensive consideration of threats and their impacts across different use cases. One participant noted the specific example of performing vulnerability analysis on a product and cited the need for comparable examples of threat analysis for manufacturers and customers alike to understand what should be done. Participants also noted that different products and product components have varying capabilities which influence threat boundaries and the nature of risks.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップ中の議論では、脅威の動的な性質が強調され、脅威は分野ごとではなく、それぞれの具体的な文脈の中で検討すべきだとされました。参加者は、このアプローチにより、異なるユースケース全体にわたる脅威とその影響を包括的に考慮できると指摘しました。ある参加者は、製品の脆弱性分析を行う具体例を挙げ、製造者も顧客も何をすべきかを理解できるよう、同等の脅威分析の例が必要であると述べました。参加者はまた、製品や製品コンポーネントによって機能が異なり、それが脅威の境界とリスクの性質に影響を与えると指摘しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13と一致

contents.html: The importance of establishing expected customer use cases to identify threat actors was stressed, alongside the necessity of focusing on threat modeling rather than merely adhering to prerequisites and requirements. Participants discussed what decisions go into threat modeling to help determine ‘who’ may be attacking as much as ‘what’ threat(s) manufacturers need to protect against. This prompts an examination of meaningful inputs to threat modeling considering the impact of malicious actors on protocol design and implementation.
contents.html_ja: 脅威アクターを特定するために想定される顧客のユースケースを確立することの重要性が強調され、前提条件や要件を守るだけでなく、脅威モデリングに焦点を当てる必要性も強調されました。参加者は、製造者が防御すべき「どのような」脅威かと同様に、「誰が」攻撃してくる可能性があるかを判断するために、脅威モデリングにどのような判断が入るかを論じました。これにより、悪意のある行為者がプロトコルの設計と実装に与える影響を考慮し、脅威モデリングへの有意義な入力情報を検証することになります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14と一致

contents.html: Participants also placed emphasis on proactive tracking and mitigation of vulnerabilities in connected devices with some participants noting that leveraging device-level security features can enhance threat detection and response. Discussions suggested focusing on enhancing existing system models, with a critical consideration of safety features, to address the unique threats posed by different products. Also as pointed out earlier, participants emphasized a need for a product baseline and specific security controls to address vulnerabilities comprehensively.
contents.html_ja: 参加者はまた、接続デバイスにおける脆弱性の能動的な追跡と緩和を重視し、デバイスレベルのセキュリティ機能を活用することが脅威の検知と対応を強化できると指摘する参加者もいました。議論では、異なる製品がもたらす固有の脅威に対処するために、安全機能を慎重に考慮したうえで、既存のシステムモデルの強化に注力することが提案されました。また、先に指摘されたように、参加者は、脆弱性に包括的に対処するために、製品のベースラインと具体的なセキュリティ管理策が必要であることを強調しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14と一致

contents.html: 3.4. Lifecycle Management of Connected Devices
contents.html_ja: 3.4. 接続デバイスのライフサイクル管理
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: There are market opportunities to securely design the next wave of products with cybersecurity through end of life and instill incentives into the maintenance of existing products.
contents.html_ja: 寿命末期に至るまでサイバーセキュリティを備えた次世代製品を安全に設計し、既存製品の保守にインセンティブを組み込む市場機会があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14の網掛けの太字の要点文（表1の行と同文）。表ではなく段落に直す

contents.html: Participants discussed the disconnect between the physical product lifetime and the software and cybersecurity support provided for connected devices. This gap poses a challenge for maintaining the security and functionality of devices throughout their lifecycle. The need to promote transparency around end of life timelines and the structured off-ramping of insecure devices was emphasized. Participants stressed the importance of providing clear end of life information on product web pages and at the point of purchase.
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、物理的な製品の寿命と、接続デバイスに提供されるソフトウェアおよびサイバーセキュリティのサポートとの間の乖離を論じました。このギャップは、デバイスのライフサイクル全体を通じてセキュリティと機能を維持するうえでの課題となります。寿命終了時期に関する透明性を高め、安全でないデバイスを計画的に段階的廃止へ移行させる必要性が強調されました。参加者は、製品のウェブページと購入時点で、明確な寿命終了情報を提供することの重要性を強調しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14と一致

contents.html: A major concern raised was the lack of industry incentives for maintaining connected devices in maintenance mode. Current business models often do not support the long-term security and maintenance of these products. The workshop highlighted that this problem exists with consumer products as well as for customers of OT products with long life cycles and high replacement costs.
contents.html_ja: 提起された大きな懸念は、接続デバイスを保守モードで維持するための産業界のインセンティブがないことでした。現在のビジネスモデルは、これらの製品の長期的なセキュリティと保守を支えていないことが多くあります。ワークショップでは、この問題が消費者向け製品だけでなく、ライフサイクルが長く交換コストが高い OT 製品の顧客にも存在することが強調されました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14と一致

contents.html: The importance of end of life product communication and management was emphasized, with participants noting that consumers struggle to find end of life dates for their connected devices. Proactive notifications, including vulnerability disclosures and off-ramping options, were deemed essential for managing these products effectively. Addressing IoT security vulnerabilities, enhancing segmentation, and disclosure practices were also key discussion points.
contents.html_ja: 寿命末期を迎える製品に関するコミュニケーションと管理の重要性が強調され、消費者が接続デバイスの寿命末期日を見つけるのに苦労していると参加者は指摘しました。脆弱性の開示や段階的廃止に向けた選択肢を含む事前通知は、これらの製品を効果的に管理するために不可欠とされました。IoT のセキュリティ脆弱性への対処、セグメンテーションの強化、開示の実践も、主要な議論のポイントでした。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14と一致

contents.html: Furthermore, this workshop emphasized the need for designing secure products with a focus on long-term updates and maintenance. Participants recognized that current business models must evolve to incorporate and appropriately prioritize security and support. Incentives for companies to prioritize cybersecurity include brand reputation and customer trust. Ensuring reliable access to physical parts and implementing secure practices, such as code signing for over-the-air updates, were identified as critical steps. The collective action required to address the issue of "zombie devices"(as defined by one of the speakers) was also highlighted as a significant concern.
contents.html_ja: さらに、このワークショップは、長期的な更新と保守に重点を置いて、安全な製品を設計する必要性を強調しました。参加者は、現在のビジネスモデルが、セキュリティとサポートを組み込んで適切に優先するように進化しなければならないと認識しました。企業がサイバーセキュリティを優先するインセンティブには、ブランドの評判と顧客の信頼があります。物理部品への確実なアクセスを確保することや、無線（over-the-air）更新のコード署名などの安全な実践を実施することが、重要なステップとして特定されました。「ゾンビデバイス」（講演者の一人による定義）の問題に対処するために必要な集団的な行動も、重大な懸念として強調されました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14〜p15にまたがる段落と一致（"zombie devices"(as の空白欠けは原本どおり）

contents.html: 3.5. Incentivizing Security Improvements
contents.html_ja: 3.5. セキュリティ改善へのインセンティブ付与
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: The balance of shared responsibility between manufacturers and users for improving security varies by sector and needs the right incentives for both.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティ向上のために製造者と利用者が分担する責任のバランスは分野によって異なり、双方に適切なインセンティブが必要です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15の網掛けの太字の要点文（表1の行と同文）。表ではなく段落に直す

contents.html: Participants explored various approaches to drive security improvements across all ecosystem participants. One primary focus was on balancing security requirements with cost and usability considerations. It was noted that while security is critical, it often comes with additional negative impacts to product usability. Participants noted the need to strike the right balance to ensure widespread adoption of security practices without compromising user experience.
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、エコシステムのすべての参加者にわたってセキュリティの改善を促すためのさまざまなアプローチを探りました。主な焦点の一つは、セキュリティ要件と、コストおよび使いやすさの考慮事項とのバランスをとることでした。セキュリティは重要ですが、製品の使いやすさに追加の悪影響を伴うことが多いと指摘されました。参加者は、ユーザー体験を損なうことなくセキュリティの実践を広く採用してもらうために、適切なバランスをとる必要があると指摘しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15と一致

contents.html: A significant point of discussion centered around questions of consumer willingness to pay for security features. Participants argued that there is often a reluctance among consumers to invest in security, which underscores the need for expanded consumer education. It was highlighted that educating consumers about the value and benefits of security features could help shift perceptions and increase their willingness to pay for these enhancements.
contents.html_ja: 議論では、消費者がセキュリティ機能に対価を支払う意思があるかどうかが重要な論点となりました。参加者は、消費者にはセキュリティへの投資をためらう傾向がしばしばあり、消費者教育の拡充が必要であることを示していると主張しました。セキュリティ機能の価値と利点について消費者を教育することは、認識を変え、こうした機能強化に対価を支払う意思を高める助けとなり得ると強調されました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15と一致

contents.html: From a product development perspective, some participants highlighted the lack of incentives to prioritize security unless driven by regulations. One participant pointed out that without regulatory pressure, manufacturers may not make end of life investments into their products or take other long-term security measures. Therefore, while market-driven incentives are valuable, regulatory approaches may be necessary to ensure comprehensive security improvements.
contents.html_ja: 製品開発の観点から、規制に促されない限りセキュリティを優先するインセンティブがないことを指摘した参加者もいました。ある参加者は、規制の圧力がなければ、製造者は製品の寿命末期への投資や、その他の長期的なセキュリティ対策を行わないかもしれないと指摘しました。したがって、市場主導のインセンティブは価値がありますが、包括的なセキュリティ改善を確保するには、規制によるアプローチが必要となる場合があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15と一致

contents.html: There was also emphasis on manufacturers relaying security information clearly and effectively, potentially leveraging data sharing between retailers and manufacturers. This approach could help bridge gaps and ensure customers are well-informed about the security features and updates related to their products. Customers who are better-informed about cybersecurity may have a greater incentive to look for cybersecurity features in products.
contents.html_ja: 製造者がセキュリティ情報を明確かつ効果的に伝えることも重視され、小売業者と製造者の間のデータ共有を活用できる可能性があります。このアプローチは、ギャップを埋め、顧客が自分の製品に関連するセキュリティ機能と更新について十分な情報を得られるようにする助けとなり得ます。サイバーセキュリティについてより多くの情報を得ている顧客は、製品のサイバーセキュリティ機能を探す動機がより強くなる可能性があります。

contents.html: 3.6. Integrating Privacy into IoT Security
contents.html_ja: 3.6. IoT セキュリティへのプライバシーの統合
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: There are broad challenges to integrating privacy objectives into IoT cybersecurity risk management.
contents.html_ja: プライバシーの目標を IoT サイバーセキュリティのリスクマネジメントに統合するには、広範な課題があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15の網掛けの太字の要点文（表1の行と同文）。表ではなく段落に直す

contents.html: Participants discussed the relationship between privacy and cybersecurity risks within IoT systems, recognizing the need to address unintended consequences from data collection and data processing. Emphasis was placed in the discussion on integrating privacy objectives like predictability, manageability, and disassociability into IoT systems while balancing these with security and operational requirements. The unique challenges of IoT, such as the extensive scale of data processing that often exceeds the original intended scope, were highlighted. Obtaining consent for all data processing activities and limiting data collection to meet user privacy preferences were noted as challenges.
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、IoT システム内のプライバシーリスクとサイバーセキュリティリスクの関係を論じ、データ収集とデータ処理から生じる意図しない結果に対処する必要性を認識しました。議論では、予測可能性、管理可能性、非関連付け性（disassociability）などのプライバシーの目標を、セキュリティと運用上の要件とのバランスをとりながら、IoT システムに統合することが重視されました。当初想定した範囲をしばしば超える大規模なデータ処理など、IoT 特有の課題が強調されました。すべてのデータ処理活動について同意を得ることや、ユーザーのプライバシー上の希望を満たすためにデータ収集を制限することが、課題として指摘されました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15と一致

contents.html: The discussion also distinguished between privacy compliance and risk management, asserting that privacy engineering presents a broader challenge that should be addressed separately from cybersecurity outcomes like those in NIST IR 8425 and required for the US Cyber Trust Mark. The discussion highlighted that privacy considerations need to be embedded in technical design requirements to effectively mitigate risks. Participants advocated for the use of an established taxonomy and terminology for consistency and clarity
contents.html_ja: 議論ではまた、プライバシーコンプライアンスとリスクマネジメントが区別され、プライバシーエンジニアリングは、NIST IR 8425 にあるような、また US Cyber Trust Mark に必要とされるサイバーセキュリティの成果とは別に取り組むべき、より広範な課題であると主張されました。議論では、リスクを効果的に緩和するために、プライバシーに関する考慮事項を技術的な設計要件に組み込む必要があることが強調されました。参加者は、一貫性と明確さのために、確立された分類法と用語を使うことを提唱しました
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p16と一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: 英文も文末が未完で、訳にも句点はない

contents.html: The importance of privacy engineering and incorporating technical design requirements was also emphasized. Participants asked for clear, robust examples and informative references within documents to support best practices. Participants also highlighted the need for using an established taxonomy and terminology for consistency and clarity when discussing privacy. Participants also pointed out that a comprehensive understanding of the data processing ecosystem's complexity and interconnectedness is vital for integrating privacy objectives. This includes maintaining confidentiality, integrity, and availability in IoT, and proactively managing privacy risks.
contents.html_ja: プライバシーエンジニアリングの重要性と、技術的な設計要件を取り入れることの重要性も強調されました。参加者は、ベストプラクティスを支えるために、文書内に明確で堅牢な例と有益な参照を含めるよう求めました。参加者はまた、プライバシーを論じる際に、一貫性と明確さのために確立された分類法と用語を使う必要性も強調しました。さらに参加者は、プライバシーの目標を統合するには、データ処理エコシステムの複雑さと相互接続性を包括的に理解することが不可欠だと指摘しました。これには、IoT における機密性、完全性、可用性の維持と、プライバシーリスクの能動的な管理が含まれます。

contents.html: 3.7. Shared Responsibility for Cybersecurity
contents.html_ja: 3.7. サイバーセキュリティにおける責任の共有
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p16の節見出し（番号は画像なので補う）

contents.html: There is an increased awareness for evolving cybersecurity responsibilities across the players of the IoT ecosystem from manufacturers to users of the ecosystem.
contents.html_ja: 製造者から利用者まで、IoT エコシステムの関係者全体で、進化するサイバーセキュリティ上の責任への認識が高まっています。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p16の網掛けの太字の要点文（表1の行と同文）。表ではなく段落に直す

contents.html: Participants indicated the importance of manufacturers communicating what customers can and need to do to maintain the cybersecurity of IoT products especially when there is an action to be taken. This includes notifications about security updates and support requirements for maintaining the product’s security.
contents.html_ja: 参加者は、IoT 製品のサイバーセキュリティを維持するために顧客ができること、また必要とされることを、特に行動が必要な場合に、製造者が伝えることの重要性を指摘しました。これには、セキュリティ更新に関する通知や、製品のセキュリティを維持するためのサポート要件が含まれます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p16と一致

contents.html: For example, including a real time assessment with a notification could help to better understand the risk such as notifying customers of a needed update and that failure to perform the update would leave the product in a downgraded cybersecurity state.
contents.html_ja: たとえば、通知にリアルタイムの評価を含めることは、リスクをより適切に理解する助けとなり得ます。たとえば、更新が必要であることと、更新を行わないと製品がサイバーセキュリティの低下した状態になることを顧客に通知する場合です。

contents.html: There was a suggestion that research into the needs and wants of consumers with respect to cybersecurity communication is needed. Abstract

This report summarizes the feedback received by the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things (IoT) program at the in-person and hybrid workshop on "Updating Manufacturer Guidance for Securable Connected Product Development" held in December 2024. The purpose of this workshop was to consider how to update Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers (NIST Internal Report (IR) 8259) based on concepts in risk management, operational technology concerns, product end of life concerns and recent trends in IoT cybersecurity and privacy. Over time, the NIST volume of work has built upon the concepts introduced in NIST IR 8259,to add technical (NIST IR 8259A) and nontechnical (NIST IR 8259B) concepts to help manufacturers and customers consider the cybersecurity of IoT devices. The NIST IR 8259 series has been used to inform and develop subsequent publications that elaborate on IoT cybersecurity across sectors and use cases (e.g., federal agency uses cases reflected in NIST SP 800-213 and consumer use cases reflected in NIST IR 8425 and the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark).

1. Introduction

On December 4th, 2024, NIST hosted a workshop titled “Workshop on Updating Manufacturer Guidance for Securable Connected Product Development” to introduce and discuss potential areas to update as the NIST Cybersecurity for Internet of Things (IoT) program revises Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers, NIST IR 8259. The workshop was structured into two portions: a morning colloquium of plenary speakers and afternoon discussion sessions to dive deeper into the topics highlighted in the morning. The workshop yielded many discussions and significant feedback for NIST. This report summarizes what was discussed at the workshop and provides these insights to the broader public.
The table of takeaways below illustrates the takeaways from the workshop from Section 3.
Table 1 - Table of Takeaways

1. Government actions to support strengthening IoT cybersecurity need to be coordinated with industry. 2. The use of robust frameworks and the adoption of open standards are crucial for effectively managing risks across heterogeneous environments. 3. The dynamic nature of threats requires more context aware inputs, more proactive tracking and mitigation measures, and more examination into the inputs of the threat modeling approach. 4. There are market opportunities to securely design the next wave of products with cybersecurity through end of life and instill incentives into the maintenance of existing products. 5. The balance of shared responsibility between manufacturers and users for improving security varies by sector and needs the right incentives for both. 6. There are broad challenges to integrating privacy objectives into IoT cybersecurity risk management. 7. There is an increased awareness for evolving cybersecurity responsibilities across the players of the IoT ecosystem from manufacturers to users of the ecosystem.

original_blocks.html: About the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things Program

The mission of the NIST Cybersecurity for the Internet of Things (IoT) program is to cultivate trust in the IoT and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale through standards, guidelines, and related tools.

The Cybersecurity for IoT program supports the development and application of standards, guidelines, and related tools to improve the cybersecurity of connected devices and the environments in which they are deployed. The program collaborates with stakeholders across government, industry, international bodies, and academia.
Background

In May 2020, NIST published Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers (NIST IR 8259), which describes recommended cybersecurity activities that manufacturers should consider integrating into their product development and support lifecycle. These foundational cybersecurity activities can help manufacturers lessen the cybersecurity-related efforts needed by customers, which in turn can reduce the prevalence and severity of IoT device compromises and the attacks performed using compromised devices.

Over time, the NIST volume of work has built upon the concepts introduced in the NIST IR 8259 series to introduce technical, IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline (NIST IR 8259A) and nontechnical, IoT Non-Technical Supporting Capability Core Baseline (NIST IR 8259B) concepts to help manufacturers and customers consider the cybersecurity of IoT devices. The NIST IR 8259 series has been used to inform and develop subsequent publications that elaborate on IoT cybersecurity across sectors and use cases (e.g., federal agency uses cases reflected in IoT Device Cybersecurity Guidance for the Federal Government: Establishing IoT Device Cybersecurity Requirements (NIST SP 800-213) and consumer use cases reflected in Profile of the IoT Core Baseline for Consumer IoT Products (NIST IR 8425) and the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark).

NIST IR 8259 serves as a foundational document for these publications—providing these a conceptual and contextual basis. But in the extension of the documents over time, these subsequent publications introduced new concepts which would benefit the broader community in the foundational NIST IR 8259 series.
About the Workshop

The purpose of this workshop was to consider how to better align NIST IR 8259 with concepts introduced in later publications. For example, NIST IR 8425 explicitly discusses IoT products and the relationship among product components. NIST IR 8259 needs to align with these concepts. Additionally, some topics have consistently come up in discussions with the community that NIST considers as potential areas to add to a revision of NIST IR 8259, including:

Broaden the discussions from a focus on the IoT system device component to considerations of entire IoT products (and connected products) to better reflect the wide variety of applications and use cases that exist.
Develop the relationship between risk assessment and threat modeling activities.
Address the different cybersecurity considerations among Information Technology (IT), Internet of Things (IoT), Operational Technology (OT), and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT)

Identify insights, considerations, approaches, etc. for IoT based on the NIST Privacy Framework, NIST Cyber Physical Systems/IoT Framework, NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, and the NIST Secure Software Development Framework.
Incorporate lessons learned and techniques developed in the execution of several IoT-related National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) projects.
Address emerging connected product technologies more directly (i.e., Immersive Tech, Artificial Intelligence).
Discuss any relationship that may exist between the repairability of connected products and cybersecurity.

Provide guidelines on balancing cybersecurity with device support considerations, especially when there is a significant mismatch between the expected end of support of the IT components and the end of life of the mechanical components of the connected products.

original_blocks.html: 2. Speaker Summaries
The summaries below highlight significant points from the speakers and identifies discussion topics.
Jack Cyprus and David Keppler, MITRE Corporation, presented ‘Building More Secure Devices Using Threat Modeling with MITRE EMB3D’

David Keppler and Jack Cyprus, both from the MITRE Corporation, discussed building more secure devices through threat modeling with MITRE EMB3D1. They emphasized that threat modeling is crucial for identifying potential vulnerabilities and determining appropriate security measures. This process, which is increasingly used in industries such as industrial automation, automotive, and medical, involves defining the device, identifying key components and trust boundaries, and measuring the return on investment (ROI) of defenses.

There are various tools and processes for threat modeling, such as adversary models and attack trees. One prominent model, the MITRE EMB3D, fills gaps in existing data sources and offers a consistent understanding of threats and mitigations. This model categorizes threats based on device properties, such as hardware, system software, application software, and networking. It also includes references to the CWE and CVE databases for additional information and threat details.

The EMB3D model provides a common language for device vendors, users, and security researchers to communicate threats and mitigations. It includes three mitigation tiers— foundational, intermediate, and leading—that guide actions throughout a device's lifecycle. These mitigations are grounded in real-world information and provide a defensive starting point as well as steps for ongoing security improvements. By adopting a comprehensive threat modeling process like EMB3D, organizations can better protect their devices against potential threats and build more secure systems.
Matthew Rogers, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), presented, ‘Secure by Design considerations for OT’

Matthew Rogers from CISA presented on the agency’s Secure-By-Design pledge 2and related efforts. Secure-by-design incentivizes security professionals to drive meaningful security changes and equips consumers with the knowledge to demand necessary security features. Establishing a secure and upgradeable foundation is crucial to avoid legacy infrastructure issues. Shared responsibility between asset owners and device manufacturers is essential, as software vulnerabilities are increasing and basic, preventable vulnerabilities can cause significant harm.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) introduced the 'Secure-By-Design' Pledge, with over 200 software manufacturers committing to deploy more secure products. Secure-by-design goals focus on secure software development and basic security functionality.
1 See MITRE EMB3d at https://emb3d.mitre.org/
2 See CISA Secure-by-Design Pledge at https://www.cisa.gov/securebydesign/pledge

Security is a collective responsibility involving manufacturers, integrators, and asset owners and operators. CISA helps clarify security roles and ensures all parties uphold their responsibilities. The key component of secure by design is seeing where manufacturers can embed cyber security from the start to make it more difficult or impossible for an integrator or asset owner to open a cyber security risk.

Current US critical infrastructure contains legacy systems without security functionality that inherently complicate adding security today. Infrastructure improvement options include the present ‘Bubble Boy’ method, which segments all traffic, targeted improvements, and the 'rip and replace' method. Secure operational technology (OT) devices need to be available to provide that defense in depth, so that any failures in segmentation do not result in total compromise. Secure-by-design for OT considers threat categories like vulnerability handling and data protection. It emphasizes open standards and autonomy at the asset and operator level. Resilience features should resemble those in the enterprise space, including secure communications, resilience, logging, and end-device capabilities.
Stacey Higginbotham, Fellow with Consumer Reports, presented, ‘Life in Maintenance Mode: What it means to keep connected devices secure.’

Stacey Higginbotham of Consumer Reports noted that connected devices establish an ongoing relationship between the buyer, seller, and manufacturer. The lifetime of a connected product is often separate from its physical state. While physical products fail in visible ways, software degrades more quickly, often without consumer awareness. The industry also lacks adequate support for maintenance. Stacey’s discussion highlighted three key areas: zombie hordes of end of life devices, supported devices with unsupportive owners, and herd immunity against malicious actors.

“Zombie devices” are those that no longer receive software support and security updates. Higginbotham noted that unsupportive owners can neglect cybersecurity issues, leading to vulnerabilities. Herd immunity in cybersecurity requires collective action from manufacturers and consumers. Most consumers are unaware or indifferent to the end of life status of their products, resulting in “zombie hordes”. Communicating end of life status and dates is crucial, including proactive notification to consumers, retailers, and third parties. Companies should track devices to address critical vulnerabilities and create structured options for off-ramping zombie devices.

Higginbotham emphasized that company priorities often overlook device security. Manufacturers should implement vulnerability disclosure programs, track issues, conduct comprehensive security audits, and allocate budgets for security maintenance. Buyers must keep products updated or segmented, and legislation should clarify responsibility to ensure herd immunity. Companies should have a dedicated point of contact for security researchers and consider recalls for insecure devices. Stacey also addressed secure repairs, both before and after end of life. Good hardware should not end up in landfills, but unpatched zombie devices pose risks. Consumer Reports advocates for designing products for longevity, including features like hardware upgrades, crypto agility, and increased memory.
Dylan Gilbert, NIST Privacy Engineering Program Lead, presented, ‘Getting Smart: An Overview of IoT Privacy’.

Privacy is a complex and evolving concept that safeguards important values like human autonomy and dignity. It reflects various factors and individual preferences and is highly context-specific, differing between public and private activities. Effective privacy risk management must consider these contexts and the various ways to achieve privacy, such as seclusion, limiting observation, and controlling facets of identity.

Gilbert emphasized that privacy could drive innovation and serve as a market differentiator. However, organizations need to have honest and risk-informed discussions about how best to balance optimizing data utility while protecting individuals’ privacy, particularly in cases where privacy risk interacts with other risk domains such as cybersecurity. The NIST Privacy Framework helps organizations understand the relationship between privacy and cybersecurity risks in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT). Problematic data actions, such as deriving inferences about individuals, can pose significant privacy risks, particularly in consumer IoT.

A key factor in managing privacy risks is an organization’s role in the data processing ecosystem, which includes the complex relationships among entities involved in data processing. An organization's role(s) in the IoT ecosystem can affect its legal obligations and the measures it should take to manage privacy risk. High-level goals for mitigating cybersecurity and privacy risks include protecting device security, data security, and individual privacy. The privacy engineering objectives of predictability, manageability, and disassociability can be useful to meet these goals by supporting the determination of privacy capabilities in IoT products.

Gilbert also discussed specific privacy risks related to IoT, such as interactions with the physical world leading to reputational harm or safety issues. Data processing might exceed the product's intended scope, and access, management, and monitoring features could result in loss of trust and economic loss. Additionally, privacy capability availability, efficiency, and effectiveness are crucial to prevent issues like discrimination and to maintain trust. IoT products need the capabilities to support configurations such as remote activation, prevention, and data minimization.
3. Workshop Takeaways
This section summarizes the takeaways and observations across the entire workshop from plenary presentations to breakout sessions.

The following takeaways are the ideas, observations, and suggestions that NIST heard from workshop participants and that received significant support from attendees and/or panelists. This workshop was not a forum for developing consensus; rather, the takeaways represent recurrent themes which emerged during the event—not formal positions taken by attendees or participants. This document cannot capture every thought, opinion, and suggestion provided during the sessions. This is an attempt to capture major themes. The takeaways do not represent specific NIST recommendations or guidelines; rather, they provide important feedback to the program and serve as a basis for future conversations with the community.
Examination of Role of Government in Coordination Initiatives
Importance of Leveraging Standards and Frameworks
Addressing Emerging Threats and Vulnerabilities
Lifecycle Management of Connected Devices
Incentivizing Security Improvements
Integrating Privacy into IoT Security
Shared Responsibility for Cybersecurity
Conclusion
Government actions to support strengthening IoT cybersecurity need to be coordinated with industry.

original_blocks.html: The government plays a crucial role in strengthening IoT cybersecurity in coordination with industry, in areas such as promoting balancing security with operational needs, and consumer awareness through effective communication and education. In these efforts, the government must work collaboratively with industry stakeholders, recognizing its own limitations while providing expert support for broader cybersecurity objectives.

The speakers highlighted the government's initiatives like Secure by Design and programs like the US Cyber Trust Mark as crucial to encourage industry to balance security requirements with operational constraints in a range of environments from Operational Control (OT) to consumer products. Under such initiatives and programs, government and industry efforts need to align to ensure the effective implementation of cybersecurity measures. Participants voiced support for a unified whole-of-government approach to address the challenges posed across different sectors and use cases ensuring that security initiatives are both comprehensive and adaptable. Discussions highlighted that, while the government can support broad objectives and promote improved cybersecurity, it should be flexible concerning specific product security measures, which are the responsibility of manufacturers.

Instead, participants recommended that the government could provide top-level support for broader cybersecurity objectives, integrating planning approaches to navigate the complexities of different sectors. Tools like effective consumer education awareness campaigns may drive better security practices to ensure consumers are well-informed about cybersecurity measures as they evolve. Participants agreed that one key aspect of government involvement is effective communication, which the participants agreed should be action-based messages directed at consumers. For example, simplifying communication and facilitating customer outreach are ways to promote awareness and understanding of cybersecurity practices. Government-led programs for consumer education were seen as vital by the audience in driving consumer engagement and encouraging consumers to value secure products. It was noted that “one size fits all communications” does not address the varying levels of knowledge in the general public.

Broad understanding of cybersecurity information and what to do with it is essential for improvement in U.S. cybersecurity. This means tailoring the message to the expected audience and collaborating with industry to move toward a more robust cybersecurity ecosystem.

Throughout the workshop, the importance of established frameworks and open standards was discussed as beneficial to enhancing IoT security and reducing threats. Real-world examples showcased how these tools can effectively mitigate cybersecurity threats while considering interactions between mitigations and device properties. It was noted that there are emerging examples of standards organizations using threat frameworks to discuss risk management.

Open standards were discussed as crucial in fostering interoperability and resilience, particularly within OT and ICS environments. Participants underscored the value of standards in making vulnerability advisories more actionable through enhanced communication across various systems. The need for clear, informative references and robust use case examples was also highlighted, emphasizing their role in clarifying specific points and supporting industry best practices.

As topics of discussion, privacy compliance and risk management emerged as important yet distinct areas of focus. The discussions noted the challenges in defining authority for privacy and managing privacy risks and the value of frameworks such as the NIST Privacy Framework to address these challenges. Additionally, there was a recognized need for a product baseline and specific security controls at varying levels to enhance overall cybersecurity efforts. Participants noted that clear and direct communication, along with formalized sections within documents, would further support the effective implementation of best practices and ensure a comprehensive approach to cybersecurity.

During the workshop, discussions highlighted the dynamic nature of threats, emphasizing that threats should be examined within their specific contexts rather than by sector. Participants noted that this approach ensures a comprehensive consideration of threats and their impacts across different use cases. One participant noted the specific example of performing vulnerability analysis on a product and cited the need for comparable examples of threat analysis for manufacturers and customers alike to understand what should be done. Participants also noted that different products and product components have varying capabilities which influence threat boundaries and the nature of risks.

The importance of establishing expected customer use cases to identify threat actors was stressed, alongside the necessity of focusing on threat modeling rather than merely adhering to prerequisites and requirements. Participants discussed what decisions go into threat modeling to help determine ‘who’ may be attacking as much as ‘what’ threat(s) manufacturers need to protect against. This prompts an examination of meaningful inputs to threat modeling considering the impact of malicious actors on protocol design and implementation.

Participants also placed emphasis on proactive tracking and mitigation of vulnerabilities in connected devices with some participants noting that leveraging device-level security features can enhance threat detection and response. Discussions suggested focusing on enhancing existing system models, with a critical consideration of safety features, to address the unique threats posed by different products. Also as pointed out earlier, participants emphasized a need for a product baseline and specific security controls to address vulnerabilities comprehensively.

Participants discussed the disconnect between the physical product lifetime and the software and cybersecurity support provided for connected devices. This gap poses a challenge for maintaining the security and functionality of devices throughout their lifecycle. The need to promote transparency around end of life timelines and the structured off-ramping of insecure devices was emphasized. Participants stressed the importance of providing clear end of life information on product web pages and at the point of purchase.

A major concern raised was the lack of industry incentives for maintaining connected devices in maintenance mode. Current business models often do not support the long-term security and maintenance of these products. The workshop highlighted that this problem exists with consumer products as well as for customers of OT products with long life cycles and high replacement costs.

The importance of end of life product communication and management was emphasized, with participants noting that consumers struggle to find end of life dates for their connected devices. Proactive notifications, including vulnerability disclosures and off-ramping options, were deemed essential for managing these products effectively. Addressing IoT security vulnerabilities, enhancing segmentation, and disclosure practices were also key discussion points.

Participants explored various approaches to drive security improvements across all ecosystem participants. One primary focus was on balancing security requirements with cost and usability considerations. It was noted that while security is critical, it often comes with additional negative impacts to product usability. Participants noted the need to strike the right balance to ensure widespread adoption of security practices without compromising user experience.

A significant point of discussion centered around questions of consumer willingness to pay for security features. Participants argued that there is often a reluctance among consumers to invest in security, which underscores the need for expanded consumer education. It was highlighted that educating consumers about the value and benefits of security features could help shift perceptions and increase their willingness to pay for these enhancements.

From a product development perspective, some participants highlighted the lack of incentives to prioritize security unless driven by regulations. One participant pointed out that without regulatory pressure, manufacturers may not make end of life investments into their products or take other long-term security measures. Therefore, while market-driven incentives are valuable, regulatory approaches may be necessary to ensure comprehensive security improvements.

There was also emphasis on manufacturers relaying security information clearly and effectively, potentially leveraging data sharing between retailers and manufacturers. This approach could help bridge gaps and ensure customers are well-informed about the security features and updates related to their products. Customers who are better-informed about cybersecurity may have a greater incentive to look for cybersecurity features in products.

Participants discussed the relationship between privacy and cybersecurity risks within IoT systems, recognizing the need to address unintended consequences from data collection and data processing. Emphasis was placed in the discussion on integrating privacy objectives like predictability, manageability, and disassociability into IoT systems while balancing these with security and operational requirements. The unique challenges of IoT, such as the extensive scale of data processing that often exceeds the original intended scope, were highlighted. Obtaining consent for all data processing activities and limiting data collection to meet user privacy preferences were noted as challenges.

The discussion also distinguished between privacy compliance and risk management, asserting that privacy engineering presents a broader challenge that should be addressed separately from cybersecurity outcomes like those in NIST IR 8425 and required for the US Cyber Trust Mark. The discussion highlighted that privacy considerations need to be embedded in technical design requirements to effectively mitigate risks. Participants advocated for the use of an established taxonomy and terminology for consistency and clarity

The importance of privacy engineering and incorporating technical design requirements was also emphasized. Participants asked for clear, robust examples and informative references within documents to support best practices. Participants also highlighted the need for using an established taxonomy and terminology for consistency and clarity when discussing privacy. Participants also pointed out that a comprehensive understanding of the data processing ecosystem's complexity and interconnectedness is vital for integrating privacy objectives. This includes maintaining confidentiality, integrity, and availability in IoT, and proactively managing privacy risks.

Participants indicated the importance of manufacturers communicating what customers can and need to do to maintain the cybersecurity of IoT products especially when there is an action to be taken. This includes notifications about security updates and support requirements for maintaining the product’s security.

For example, including a real time assessment with a notification could help to better understand the risk such as notifying customers of a needed update and that failure to perform the update would leave the product in a downgraded cybersecurity state.

There was a suggestion that research into the needs and wants of consumers with respect to cybersecurity communication is needed. One option would be to run focus groups with consumers including those with limited background on cybersecurity. More research could lead to making communications more effective. This led to the question: what should be highlighted as specific actions from the manufacturer to the customer and what responsibility lies with the customer? It was noted that this observation may have different answers in some use cases (e.g., consumer sector) compared to others (e.g., OT and enterprise).

NIST heard that effective risk management in the IoT ecosystem requires a balanced approach that aligns industry needs with government capabilities; that utilizing robust frameworks, open standards, and context-aware inputs is vital for tracking and mitigating dynamic threats; that addressing the lifecycle of products and evolving cybersecurity responsibilities among all stakeholders are crucial elements; that enhanced coordination and innovative approaches in IoT cybersecurity can significantly improve risk management and security incentives which ultimately benefit both manufacturers and users.

NIST looks forward to joining industry for a follow-up workshop in March on risk management and threat modeling to obtain more feedback on the continuation of the discussion topics of this workshop and to gather more in-depth insights from the collaboration of the community on updating manufacturer guidelines for securable connected product development.

Furthermore, this workshop emphasized the need for designing secure products with a focus on long-term updates and maintenance. Participants recognized that current business models must evolve to incorporate and appropriately prioritize security and support. Incentives for companies to prioritize cybersecurity include brand reputation and customer trust. Ensuring reliable access to physical parts and implementing secure practices, such as code signing for over-the-air updates, were identified as critical steps. The collective action required to address the issue of "zombie devices"(as defined by one of the speakers) was also highlighted as a significant concern.
This workshop was a productive conversation that yielded many discussions and significant feedback for the NIST Cybersecurity for IoT Program to consider for the revision of NIST IR

The morning plenary sessions began with discussions on building more secure devices using threat modeling, examining secure by design considerations for OT, examining the maintenance outlook on devices after end of life requirements, and examining how privacy implications extend beyond traditional IT into IoT. The afternoon breakout sessions featured participant discussions of topics on questions aligned to the pre-market and post-market activities of NIST IR 8259.
